question: Tell me about a time you delivered something under a tight deadline.
answer: In my third year, our capstone team had five days to deliver a working demo after our backend API broke a week before the submission. I rewrote the two failing endpoints overnight myself, cut the report-export feature as a scoped-down trade-off, and told our guide about the change the same day so there were no surprises. We demoed on time, and the guide rated our project the best of the nine teams in the batch.

question: Your final-year demo is a week away and a teammate has gone silent. What do you do?
answer: I would call him directly that evening rather than wait another day, because silence usually means he is stuck, not lazy. If he is still unreachable by the next morning, I take over his two modules myself and ask our guide for one volunteer from a parallel project group. I have done this before — during our tech-fest build I absorbed a teammate's payment-integration work in two days — so I know the demo will not slip.

question: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list.
expected_answer_points: array elements sit in contiguous memory so indexing is O(1)
linked list nodes are scattered and connected by pointers so access is O(n)
insertion or deletion at a known position is O(1) in a linked list but O(n) in an array due to shifting
arrays are cache-friendly while list nodes pay extra pointer memory per element
answer: An array stores its elements in contiguous memory, so any index can be reached directly in O(1) time by address arithmetic. A linked list stores nodes scattered in memory connected through pointers, so reaching the k-th element means walking from the head, which costs O(n). Insertion or deletion at a position you already hold is O(1) in a linked list, while an array needs O(n) shifting of the following elements. Arrays are also cache-friendly and compact, whereas every list node pays extra pointer storage per element.
note: all four expected points covered precisely, correct terminology

question: What is overfitting and how do you prevent it?
expected_answer_points: overfitting means the model memorises training noise and fails to generalise to unseen data
it is detected when training accuracy keeps rising while validation accuracy drops
prevention includes regularisation such as L1/L2 or dropout
more training data, cross-validation and early stopping also reduce it
answer: Overfitting is when a model learns the training data so well, including its noise, that it stops generalising to unseen data. You usually detect it by comparing training and validation curves: training accuracy keeps improving while validation accuracy starts falling. To prevent it I would use regularisation like L2 weight decay or dropout, get more training data where possible, use k-fold cross-validation, and stop training early once the validation loss stops improving.
note: definition, detection, and both prevention points all covered

question: Explain normalization in a DBMS.
expected_answer_points: normalization decomposes tables to remove redundancy and update anomalies
1NF removes repeating groups so each cell holds one atomic value
2NF removes partial dependency of non-key attributes on part of a composite key
3NF removes transitive dependency of non-key attributes on other non-key attributes
answer: Normalization means breaking one large table into smaller related tables so that the same data is not stored twice and anomalies during update or delete are avoided. First normal form requires each field to hold a single atomic value. The higher normal forms, like 2NF and 3NF, then progressively remove partial and transitive dependencies on the key, though I don't remember the exact boundary conditions of each one.
note: first two points covered, 2NF/3NF only named as concepts — coverage cap lands the holistic near 7

question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
expected_answer_points: SQL injection is attacker-supplied input being interpreted as SQL by the application
it typically happens when user input is concatenated directly into a query string
parameterised queries or prepared statements separate code from data and prevent it
least-privilege DB accounts and input validation or escaping add defence in depth
answer: SQL injection is an attack where the attacker manages to give input that the database executes as part of the query, and it usually happens when the application joins user input directly into the query string. The standard defence is to use parameterised queries or prepared statements so the input is always treated as data instead of code.
note: three of four points covered cleanly, defence-in-depth point missed — completeness 8.5, coverage cap 8

question: Explain precision and recall.
expected_answer_points: precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive: TP over (TP plus FP)
recall is the fraction of actual positives that were found: TP over (TP plus FN)
precision penalises false positives while recall penalises false negatives
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall
answer: Precision and recall measure how good a classification model is. Precision means how many predictions the model got right overall, which is basically its accuracy. Recall means how many of the correct results it managed to recall from the training data. F1 score is used to combine them by taking their average.
note: precision conflated with accuracy (clearly wrong claim caps correctness at 3); recall misdefined; F1 called a plain average
